utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen in the courtroom and in the visitor's gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I apologise again today for this ten-minute delay. There are more urgent matters which have to be settled as soon as we come to the Tribunal. Mr. Harmon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge Riad. Good morning, colleagues. This morning, Mr. President, and all day today, we will not present any live witnesses. We had scheduled a witness for today but because of problems in respect of passport and securing a passport, the witness was not able to arrive in time for her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Is she arriving in the near future?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: She's now arriving today as opposed to her scheduled time of arrival which was two days ago. So in lieu of that, the Prosecutor proposes to present video testimony film of testimony that had been given in 1996 at the Rule 61 hearing involving Karadzic and Mladic. I have discussed this with my colleagues from the Defence long before today, and they have agreed that in lieu of calling the witnesses who will be shown on the videotape, they would accept the transcribed testimony and the video testimony of these same witnesses. So today we'll be presenting the testimonies of Colonel Karremans, Lieutenant Koster, and a gentleman from Bosnia named Pasaga Mesic. We will play those videotapes from the previous Rule 61 hearing and then we'll seek to admit those tapes into evidence. During the course of the presentation today, I'm going to ask my colleague, Mr. McCloskey, to remain in the courtroom as the Prosecutor's representative, and with the Court's permission I will excuse myself and return at the end of the day. So that is the agenda we have proposed for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you're on the tape too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am on the tapes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So we'll have you with us. Is Defence counsel agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, dear colleagues. The Defence agrees to the proposal made by the Prosecution so we concur that the video cassettes be viewed and admitted into the file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Fourmy. [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Fourmy is asking whether Colonel Karremans had been here before us in this trial. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He has not been in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I know he has not been here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He has not. As I said previously, I discussed this matter with the Defence and they agree that the testimony that he had given under oath previously would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Is he coming? Would he be coming?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He will not be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The tape will substitute for his live testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That answers Mr. Fourmy's question, perhaps. [Interpretation] Your preoccupations have been satisfied, Mr. Fourmy. [In English] You can proceed, please, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge Riad. If we could put the first video, the testimony of Colonel Karremans, on the screen. If I may be excused, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How long do you think it will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The video of Colonel Karremans is two hours and, I believe, twenty minutes; the video of Lieutenant Koster is 59 minutes; and the videotape of Mr. Mesic is 29 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So we can have the break after Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We, perhaps, may want to have a break in between Karremans given the fact that it's two hours and twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. We'll see to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Court reporter's note: Transcription of videotape is as follows:]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, the Tribunal accepts that evidence, all the documents, and accepts that a photograph of the map, according to the technical facilities that we have, will be added. We have now Colonel Karremans before us. We have to give him some headsets. Can you hear me, sir? Can you read the statement which you have in your hand? Can you please give Colonel Karremans some headsets. I think that you must give the headsets each time and that the usher should be told of that. Please read the statement that you have in your hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colonel. Please be seated. Can you hear me, Colonel? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Karremans, the Tribunal, dealing with Mr. Karadzic and Mladic, wanted to call upon you here so that we can see what you have to say in light of the indictment. I think it is the Office of the Prosecutor who will introduce you. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, could you please state your full name and spell your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: My last name is Karremans. I will spell that. K-a-r-r-e-m-a-n-s, Karremans. My first name is Thomas, T-h-o-m-a-s, and middle name, Jacob.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: My occupation now is that I am taking over an assignment in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a member of the Dutch military?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: I'm a member of the Dutch military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you participate in UN peacekeeping operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where were you assigned in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: I was assigned in Bosnia-Herzegovina last year, from January up to July in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were your duties and responsibilities in that particular assignment?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: My mission was -- I was the battalion commander of DutchBat in the safe area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the UN mandate that you received in relation to your assignments?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: The UN mandate especially for the safe havens or safe areas like Srebrenica was based on one of the United Nations resolutions. I can remember 819. After there was a ceasefire agreement between General Morillon and General Mladic in 1993, after that agreement, the Canadians went in in the safe area and we took over the year after that, in 1994. My assignment there was commander of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, did the Bosnian Serb army interfere or obstruct with your unit's ability to perform its mandate after you had arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: I think not at the time that we arrived but they did during our stay in the enclave during, let's say, the last five months, as of half February.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you expand on that, please.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: I can expand on that but then I have first, let's say, to explain what the mission was of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: That was twofold; one was the purely military side of the mission and the other side was the humanitarian one. The military was to look to the ceasefire agreement between both warring factions, of both parties, to assist the civil authorities in the opstina of Srebrenica, to maintain negotiations between the BSA and the BiH, and of course trying to reject the BSA from attacking the enclave. On the other hand, the humanitarian side of the mission was to support the refugees within the enclave as much as possible by medical, by food, by, let's say, the infrastructure within the enclave, to enhance that, and that was, let's say, the second part of the mission of the battalion. When we took over in January 1995, from, let's say, the second battalion, we were the third there, we had no problems, let's say, during the rotation. We had no problems in the beginning with the BSA. There were some problems with the BiH, the Bosnian forces, in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What problems developed with the Bosnian Serb military? Could you describe those, please.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Those problems started actually on the 18th of February when the last convoy came in with diesel, gas, which we needed for the performance of the mission. I can a little bit expand on that. Normally we used 4.000 to 5.000 litres a day for our vehicles for patrolling, for resupply of the observation posts, et cetera. As of the 18th of February, the last diesel convoy came in and that meant that we had to reorganise our mission, our work, because you don't -- you need that amount of fuel for doing a mission. At the end, during February, March, April, up to July, the amount of diesel we had became less and less and that meant that at the end we did all our patrolling, and this is just one example, by foot. We were not able to resupply our observation posts, we were not able to do the patrolling by cars or combat vehicles, and that meant we had to do all the patrolling by foot, with all the possible problems of the mining around and within the enclave. That was the example of diesel. At the end of April the real convoy terror, as we called it in those days, started because as of the 26th of April no convoy came in at all, and that meant no personnel which was on leave in the Netherlands came back. They were stuck in Zagreb and they never returned. Under those persons, the military from our battalion, about 180 at the end were stuck up in Zagreb. There were some quite important persons, for instance, my ops officer, a major, and most of the deputy company commanders, and some other persons working in my battalion staff. That happened as of the end of April. That meant also that at the end of April, not allowing convoys coming in, that I had no resupply of medicines for the battalion but also for the population, the refugees within the enclave, no food supplies, no spare parts for my vehicles, the weaponry, no engineer equipment to assist the opstina and the people living in the opstina for repairs of infrastructure, and no equipment to test my ammunition vehicles. That happened, let's say, until the last day I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What effect did this have on the civilian -- did the Bosnian Serb blockade have on the civilian population within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did, because almost, let's say, 25.000 persons living in the enclave were refugees, as there used to live about 8.000 in the village of Srebrenica. So you can imagine that the civil authorities had a mighty challenge to bring under all those refugees in a city with an infrastructure for only 8.000 persons. But also the food for all the people living in the enclave was a problem because the UNHCR was responsible, or at least was -- they were responsible for bringing in the food. Also the UNHCR had the same problems with getting in their food for the inhabitants of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were complaints made to the Bosnian Serb authorities about the blockade and its effects?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Yes, we did, sir. Every day, at 6.00 in the night, we sent our information, daily sitreps, to the higher echelons, and that started in sector north-east in Tuzla, going up to Sarajevo, the BH command, up to the force commander in Zagreb. They were aware of, let's say, the problems within the enclave; on one side with the battalion and on the other side with the population. We noticed that and we put all the information, let's say, on a daily basis to the higher echelons. On top of that, I have written a lot of reports during my stay over there, let's say once in two days, in describing the poor situation of the people over there. Also after the meetings we had with the local authorities, they always mentioned what their problems were towards the people. We mentioned that in our daily reports, and I mentioned that quite some times in my, let's say, own reports up to the force commander in Zagreb, and also to the Crisis Staff here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Karremans, did you have contacts with the Bosnian Serb military officials from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your contacts with those officials, did you complain to them about the effects of the blockade?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Yes. Every time when we had a meeting with, let's say, representatives of the Bosnian Serb army -- I think we will come to the persons later -- we made our complaints given by the civil authorities within the enclave, what happened with the population, not only in providing food for them but also on the medical side of the whole support for the people. In the beginning we supported the population as much as we could, in combination with MSF, Medecins Sans Frontiers, by ambulances in the area, by giving them medicines, giving them medical care, picking up wounded persons or sick persons and bring them to the hospital in Srebrenica or, if that wasn't possible, to our own field dressing station. That was, as of the end of April, also stopped. The same applied for, let's say, the normal, daily living within the enclave. All those complaints we told several times when we had meetings with representatives of the BSA to those representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was their reaction, Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you identify some of the persons in the Bosnian Serb army with whom you had contact and with whom you liaised on?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Yes, I can, sir. In the first place, and I met him in the first week when I arrived in Bosnia, in Srebrenica, I met Colonel Vukovic. He was the so-called liaison officer between the battalion and the Drina Corps commander or the Drina Corps. He was also the commander of one of the brigades, the brigade in the southern part of the surroundings of Srebrenica. The second BSA representative which we met quite often was Major Nikolic. He was the liaison officer from the Bratunac Brigade, and the Bratunac Brigade was the brigade in the northern area, outside the enclave. He was the representative of that brigade and he was also the LSO which we dealt often with. Those two persons, we met during not daily meetings but sometimes a couple of times a week, sometimes even once a month, when they liked to have a meeting and not when we liked to have a meeting. A third person I know is Petar. Petar is an interpreter who both of the just named officers used all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, during your contacts with Major Nikolic, did he ever express an opinion to you about his attitude toward the Bosnian Muslim population of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did. Actually, that was in one of the meetings, from what I can remember, in February. We had always our meetings either on OP Echo, that's an observation post in the southern part of the enclave, or OP Papa in the northern part. This was on one of the occasions which I can remember in February in which he told me, you could see it on his face too, that the hatred of the Muslim people, especially those who were living in the enclave, and he said he had a reason for that because half of his family had been murdered during the Second World War. Secondly, he told me that, in his opinion, all the Muslims should leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thirdly, I think looking in those days, at that moment to his face, that he meant that, and that there was quite some hatred in his eyes, and also in the words, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, you mentioned that a number of Dutch soldiers were stationed inside the enclave of Srebrenica. Let me show you an exhibit which is a map of the enclave. It will be presented to you and then I would like to ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have copies as well for Your Honours which I'd ask the usher to please take up to the bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, there should be a monitor in front of you that -- there should be that particular exhibit appearing in front of you on the monitor. Can you please point to the map and identify the locations where Dutch soldiers were stationed within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can. If, Your Honours, you look to the map, you can see a dotted line in there, with a "C" on top and a "B," Bravo, in the south. What we did when we took that over from the previous battalion was that we divided the area in two parts; the northern area was the responsibility of our C Company and the southern part of the area was the responsibility of the B Coy, the Bravo Company. We started off in January with eight observation posts from which we could see a great part of the area. In the beginning, in January and February, both companies had some observation posts. I start with the one here on top, OP Papa, that was the observation post I just was referring to when we had our meetings with BSA representatives. We have here OP Quebec and OP Romeo on the east side. We have OP November on the north. Those four, November, Papa, Quebec, and Romeo, belonged to the C Coy, including the Alpha observation post, so that means five observation posts when we started off. In the southern part of the enclave, OP Charlie in the west, OP Echo here in the south, and OP Foxtrot also in the south. That meant eight observation posts when I took it over. What I explained before, Your Honours, is due to the convoy terror, if I may say so, and lack of gasoline, diesel, we changed our mission, let's say, daily by daily, but especially our main mission, working from observation posts and patrolling between observation posts within the enclave to more observation posts and less patrolling by cars, and later on only patrolling by foot. We decided to build more observation posts. We did that in contact with the BiH forces inside the enclave and we also discussed that with the BSA representatives, and they all agreed to that except observation post Kilo over here, but I'd like to come to that one later on, if I may. During our stay there, we made OP Mike, OP Delta, and OP Hotel, that's the old one, and at the end of our stay, OP Hotel in the direct vicinity of the village of Srebrenica. There have been a lot of problems about OP Kilo, that was our last one, and Delta, because OP Kilo and Delta, we projected those observation posts on smuggle routes, if I may say so. During our stay, and also during the stays of both previous battalions, we noticed that there was a lot of smuggling between the safe area of Srebrenica and the safe area of Zepa, and they used a couple of routes from the southern part of the enclave, in the southern direction to Zepa. That's why we put Delta and Kilo on those routes. From the Bosnian military side, they had, let's say, quite some problems that we established those two observation posts. At the end we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Colonel Karremans, how many soldiers were stationed in each of those observation posts?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: We started in January with, let's say, ten soldiers per observation post. But after the end of April, when the left convoys didn't return to Srebrenica, and we made more observation posts and we did less patrolling, or let's say it in another way, another kind of patrolling, we changed a little bit the manning of the observation posts and went to six in some cases and ten in other cases. We had some observation posts with ten persons just for observation and doing the patrols and we had some observation posts with only six persons on it just for observation. In total, at the end of our stay, on 12 observation posts I had about 90 to 100 soldiers working day by day on the posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, had the Bosnian Serb blockade not taken place, what was the normal number of soldiers you would have had in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: The battalion consisted of 780 persons, soldiers; 180 were situated in the Tuzla area, one company, a large company, I must say, and I had 600 soldiers, including 50 of the field dressing station, at my disposal within the enclave, 600. But at the end, let's say in April, about 150 to 180 didn't return, so I had about 400, 420 soldiers at my disposal as of the end of April till the end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Of those 420 soldiers, how many of those soldiers were infantry men?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: About half; 100 on the observation posts, about 100 for doing the patrols, special patrolling in the enclave along the borders of the enclave, for the guarding of both compounds in Srebrenica itself and in Potocari, and the other 200 soldiers were all for manning the three company staffs, the battalion staff, for all the logistics and the field dressing station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So by the time the invasion started in July, less than half of your available military personnel were infantry soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court what type of weaponry was available to your troops at the time the invasion started?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Our government has chosen for a so-called light option and the weaponry we had in those days were small arms. Every soldier had his own arm, either a pistol or a light machine-gun or a rifle. Then we had light machine-guns, guns on the observation posts and also on both compounds. We had the heavy machine-guns on our armoured personnel carriers. Besides that we had six mortars, 81-millimetre. They were on the observation posts, let's say on some of the observation posts. I had at my disposal anti-tank weapons, medium range and long range, amongst them, for instance, the tow wide anti-tank systems, and some small anti-tank weapons as well. I think that is what the main armament was of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Serb army blockade of Srebrenica that started in April have any effect on the amount of ammunition or the quality of weaponry that you had at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Not really. That had already happened when we entered -- let's say the first battalion entered the enclave, because we had to work -- I gave you that example with small arms, our personal arms, which we took over from the previous battalion and they took it over from the first battalion. Those weapons, small arms, they were -- although they were maintained daily, they were used a lot. The same applied for the anti-tank systems I had. Every half a year, for instance, a tow rocket should be in a test bed. You have to test it if it works well. I didn't have that test equipment so I couldn't rely on my anti-tank weapons. Another thing is when the battalion came in, the first one, is that I had only 16 per cent of the ammunition I normally should have, and that ammunition was, after more than a year, in bad circumstances as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, did General Mladic have good intelligence about what was happening in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did. In the first place he could notice, by all the troops that he had around the enclave, what was going on within the enclave. He could say what we were doing, when we were patrolling, when we are leaving compounds with vehicles, or by patrols, when we were resupplying the observation posts. He knew everything that we did internally. Secondly, he was well aware of our supplies in the battalion because he was the person, or let's say his staff were persons who refused, especially after the end of April, refused all our convoys. And those convoys which came in, we used so-called loading papers on which you have to describe what you will have or receive. So they know exactly what was on supply in the enclave for our battalion: food, medicines, spare parts, engineering equipment, et cetera. In the third place, he was well aware of what was going on in the enclave on both sides of the battalion and also on the population and civil authorities because -- and he mentioned that to me in one of the meetings that I had with him, that he was well aware of what was going on in the enclave every day, every minute, by persons he had posted in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when the Bosnian Serb invasion of the enclave started, did the Bosnian Serb army attack the outposts that you've described?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When the invasion started in July 1995, did the BSA attack your observation posts?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: That already started in June, the 3rd of June. I'd like to recall or go back to the end of May when the air strikes were executed in the Pale area, with the result that I think over more than 300 UN soldiers were hijacked in those days. After that the problems in the safe areas of Gorazde and Zepa, with all the British and Ukrainian observation posts, and that happened also in the beginning of June. On the 1st of June, I had to come to OP Echo, that is, just at the southern part of the enclave. There was a telephone call. We had a land line between the observation post Echo and one of the posts or -- yes, one of the posts of the BSA, and it was a land line which we could use for making telephone calls when we'd like to have a meeting with them or they'd like to have a meeting with us. I used the telephone and I got the interpreter on the other end, Petar, I referred to him, and he, in the name of Vukovic, asked me to consider leaving OP Echo. I asked him for a reason which he didn't give me, and that was it. I stated that I won't leave OP Echo at all. Two days later, and that was on the 3rd of June, in the early morning, I think it was about 9.00, all of a sudden, after a warning of a couple of minutes, the BSA attacked OP Echo with about 60 soldiers heavily armed with mortars, hand grenades, with anti-tank weapons, and the manning of the observation post were ordered, under fire, to leave OP Echo. They happily succeeded in that without leaving persons behind, but they left behind a lot of equipment. What they took with them was the vehicles, the communications systems, some personal stuff, and weaponry. The rest was left on OP Echo. That was the first observation post we lost in the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, how many Dutch soldiers were manning OP Echo at the time of the attack?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: In those days?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the time of the attack.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: I think ten persons, ten soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please continue describing the attacks on the observation posts.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: After that attack, executed, what I stated before, by about 60 persons, leaving with the APC the OP Echo, we did two things, actually three: In the first place, we made an immediate report for the higher echelons what happened, what was going on. Secondly, we asked for a meeting with Colonel Vukovic or Nikolic to ask them what was going on, the purpose of that attack, that we'd like to have back the observation post and that we'd like to have back the equipment left behind on that observation post. The second thing that we did immediately after losing that observation post was establishing OP Sierra and OP Uniform, that is to say, 200, 300 metres north of OP Echo. That gave a remarkable reaction on the BSA because they, I think, didn't expect that reaction. So also we lost OP Echo. We had two observation posts nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the reaction of your Bosnian Serb liaison officer when you asked for the observation post back and for your equipment back?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: It took quite a while when we had a first meeting after the loss of OP Echo. I cannot remember when we had the first meeting after, let's say, the 3rd of June. But the reaction was that we couldn't get back the equipment and we couldn't get back the observation post at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were there additional attacks on the observation posts prior to or during the invasion of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. As a result of the attacks on the observation posts, were Dutch soldiers taken prisoners by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Not on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us on which occasions they were taken prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Yes, I can. That happened, Your Honours, on the start of -- let's say on the 6th of July, and that was already a month later. In the period between the 3rd of June, OP Echo, and the 6th of July, it was rather quiet in the area. Also there was a tense situation, I must say, but it was really quiet, except one occasion somewhere in the middle of June, what happened in the vicinity of Srebrenica itself. On the 6th of July, in the morning, about 3.00, the war started over there. It started in our area, the compound of Potocari, by shooting over the compound with some rockets. The attacks started in the southern part of the enclave, in the area of OP Foxtrot. That was on the Thursday, Thursday, the 6th of July, and those attacks were carried out, let's say, during six days. The first OP which had been attacked really by small arms, by mortars, and by tanks was OP Foxtrot; that one on Thursday, on Friday, and on Saturday. And it was on Saturday, I think by noonish or 1.00, that I ordered to retreat the manning of the OP and leave it during a pause of shootings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many men were stationed in OP Foxtrot?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Just a moment. Seven men. Seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: On Saturday, in the afternoon, when OP Foxtrot had been attacked for a third day, and I asked, I can remember, for a second time for close air support, things were going on rather quickly, because on Saturday and Sunday I lost quite some observation posts in the southern part of the enclave here. There were two possibilities for the soldiers on the observation posts -- actually, there were three possibilities: Just leave the observation post and go back to the compound; secondly, stay as long as they could, making use of defence walls, making use of the shelters within the observation post; thirdly, retreat from the observation post knowing that the BiH should make problems because they, not ordered us, but they thought that we should stay on the observation post and not retreat it or not leave them. There was another possibility: just to end up, let's say, taken away by BSA forces. In most of the cases, leaving the observation post, the last thing happened. The observation posts were attacked by BSA forces, they were encircled by forces, and the only thing soldiers could do is hand over equipment, use their vehicles, and they were sent, let's say, to Simici, or later on to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As a result of those actions by the BSA against the observation post, how many Dutch soldiers were taken into custody by the BSA and detained?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: At the end there were 55 soldiers taken in custody and detained from seven or eight different observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, those 55 soldiers were all infantry soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they were all infantry soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If my mathematics are correct, that represented about 25 per cent of your infantrymen available in the compound at the time of the invasion?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know how many Bosnian Serb army soldiers participated in the invasion of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Not at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you subsequently find out?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: Yes, because Mladic told me, General Mladic told me, at the end that he had quite some troops around the enclave of Srebrenica. Those were not the original troops around the enclave but, let's say, fresh troops, fresh brigades. He used one brigade for the attack in the southern -- from the southern direction, from south to north; he had another brigade from east to the west; and he had one brigade in reserve north of Bratunac. Bratunac is the city somewhere over here. Actually, what he told me, he had three brigades or brigade-sized units of which he used two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many men are in a brigade?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think that in every brigade there were between 1.000 and 1.500 soldiers with this heavy weaponry and other weaponry than we had in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you specifically that question: Colonel Karremans, what type of weapons were available to the invading Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: They had all the equipment from the former Yugoslavian army, at least that was left out of it. They had quite some artillery pieces. We had noticed those pieces already around the enclave during our stay over there. Sometimes they changed the position of those artillery pieces; sometimes they changed the positions of mortars they had, heavy mortars, light mortars. Quite a lot, I must say. They had some main bell tanks, the old T-55s, and even some new types which we had noticed and which they had used; some anti-aircraft vehicles which they didn't use for anti-aircraft but for the attacks on the villages in the southern part of the enclave, I mean, in direct line, and a lot of anti-tank weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they also have multiple rocket systems?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS.
utterances.text: They had a couple of multiple rocket systems, small ones, all on wheels, of which we had noticed at least three north of the compound of Potocari, around the hills. And he had, let's say, a larger multiple rocket system in the city of Bratunac which he used as well, shelling the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am looking at the clock. Perhaps this is an appropriate time to recess for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I share your view. This is a good moment to have a recess. We will stop the hearing for today, and the Tribunal will resume tomorrow at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Court reporter's note: Transcription of videotape is as follows:]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First question: Can everyone hear me? Mr. Harmon, can you hear me? Can you hear me, counsel for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Great. Can the registry hear me? Interpreters can hear me? Everybody can hear what's going on? The visitors' gallery, everyone can hear all right? No technical problem. Fellow Judges hear me? Terrific. Now, Mr. Harmon, we can proceed with Colonel Karremans' testimony, and I would ask the usher to bring him in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Karremans, good morning. You can hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So we shall resume with your testimony. You've been called by the Prosecution in the case of the Prosecution against Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, yesterday you described the Bosnian Serb army blockade that slowly strangled the enclave as a convoy of terror. What effect did this have on the occupants of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to stipulate some things which I have said yesterday concerning the circumstances, I must say, the miserable circumstances for the inhabitants of the enclave, but also for my own battalion. That could explain something on the circumstances up to the 6th of July. All those, let's say, miserable circumstances in April, May, and June were caused, what I said yesterday, by refusing the incoming convoys either for the battalion or by UNHCR for the refugees. Thus, we had to do with a strangulation of the enclave or, so to call, an isolation, a total blockade. That meant for the population, for instance, that their situation was poorer than poor. There was starvation for the refugees. Some died by starvation. There was no medical treatment at all for the population; no doctors, no dentists, no medicines. The Medecins Sans Frontiers, MSF, was not able to fulfil its job in the local hospital. We couldn't do anything about the infrastructure to support the local authorities, like housing, like generators, power and electricity, water supply for the population. It ended up, for instance, that hundreds of inhabitants of the enclave lived literally on the garbage collection point. There was no travel allowed both for the population and for the battalion. What was agreed in the beginning, in 1993, the so-called freedom of movement, there was no freedom of movement at all. Our conclusion for the inhabitants, the population of the enclave, was that the situation was hopeless, inhuman and a lot of suffering for the people. On the other side, for the battalion, I'd like to describe that a little bit too, if I may, and I'll use a couple of parameters which I also put in my reports for the higher echelons, and also for my national authorities. In the first place, the logistics, I have told you, Your Honours, a little bit about that yesterday on the diesel, the lack of diesel which implied that we have to live in the dark with my battalion for a couple of months. We had no electricity for water, for heating, and the weather conditions in those days, until the end of May, were extreme, a lot of rain day after day. So we couldn't use our vehicles, one side, because of lack of fuel, but the other side, the roads we had in the enclave, we couldn't use them. Because of the lack of diesel we had to patrol by foot, with all the consequences of the mines all over the area. There was no possibility of resupplying my observation posts, and that's why we used horses from the locals. What I said before, there was no heating especially under those extreme weather conditions. We had no medicines, we had no spare parts, we had no engineering equipment and no food, except our combat rations, and we lived on combat rations a long time. We called that in the end a logistical regime. Then of my own personnel, the soldiers, I had a lack of personnel because they couldn't enter the enclave as of the 26th of April. They got no mail from home. There was no freedom of movement. We couldn't leave the enclave; we couldn't enter the enclave. The third parameter were the operations. We had adjusted the orders for the battalion several times, and I explained that yesterday, from eight observation posts to 12, and even 13 at the end, patrolling by foot instead of using armoured personnel carriers. We made contingency plans as of, let's say, the air strikes in Pale, the end of May. Contingency plans were for the observation post one-hour notice, and one-hour notice meant that the soldiers on an observation post, after an order, should leave the observation post within an hour, and that was 24 hours a day, the time we have been there. Humanitarian support, I just explained that to you, we were not able to support the population within the enclave. One of the other parameters was the psychological effect on the soldiers, but also on the population; the morale of the battalion, but also from the population. The terrain conditions were bad and the weather conditions were even worse. That ended up on the 25th of May where I informed, in a long report to all the higher echelons and to the national authorities, that I was not able to fulfil my mission any longer. That meant end of the mission, period. Then we started with making all improvisations. Using those improvisations, we could handle the mission more or less until the 6th of July. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, based on the Bosnian Serb blockade and its effects, as well as the capture of 55 of your soldiers by the Bosnian Serb army, did you feel that you had the means to fulfil your mission?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the end. In the beginning, when we started in January, I could fulfil the mission based on the mandate, based on what I had, personnel, equipment, the incoming convoys. But at the end of my stay over there, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn your attention to the actual invasion itself. What was the effect on the civilian population once the invasion started?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, Your Honours, the invasion started on the 6th of July. It started with heavy fighting in the southern part of the enclave, in the direct vicinity of OP Foxtrot, and by shelling the city of Srebrenica itself, the compounds and some other observation posts. But actually it started in the south. In the southern part of the enclave, there was the so-called Swedish shelter project, a lot of housing built under Swedish authorities. In that Swedish shelter project there used to live about 3.000 refugees. As soon as the attacks started in the southern part, all those refugees fled in the northern direction, towards the city of Srebrenica. You can imagine there was panic, chaos, in those days, what I explained before, no food, and there was no way to give them houses in Srebrenica itself. Panic, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did the people flee to?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They fled to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they flee to the UN compound in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the beginning. That was, I think, on the 10th, on the Monday, and of course at the last day, on Tuesday, the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many refugees were in and around the UN compound in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but there must be hundreds at the compound and maybe thousands around it. They were all gathered together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened to those refugees in the compound around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have to refer to the 11th, the last day?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at that day and the days before, Srebrenica itself was already shelled quite some times. At the 11th, well, while all those refugees were gathered together, at least most of them, the BSA started shelling the city, it started shelling the compound of Srebrenica itself, and that ended up with a lot of wounded persons, death. Also in the morning and -- on the morning of the 11th, we already evacuated the local hospital and we brought all the wounded persons to the compound of Potocari. As soon as the shelling started in the afternoon of the 11th, just before the air strikes, or during the air attacks, all the refugees fled in the direction of Potocari, in the northern direction, to the compound of the battalion staff and staff company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, Colonel Karremans, some of the BSA artillery shells landed in and around the UN compound itself in Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did that cause civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That caused civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned as a result of the attacks on the city of Srebrenica itself there was a large exodus of civilians that fled to Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did those people who fled from Potocari come to the UN compound in -- I'm sorry. Did the refugees who fled from the UN compound in Srebrenica flee to the UN compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately how many people gathered in and around the UN compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just an estimation, of course, but we were forced to split up the group of refugees because there were so many thousands. We put, let's put it that way, or invited, that's a better word, we invited about 4.000 to 5.000 refugees within our own compound of Potocari, and then it was completely full, filled up, with refugees and our own personnel. Then we had another 15.000 to 20.000 persons still outside of the compound of Potocari and we used two or three shelled factories just in the vicinity of the compound of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the percentage of women to men in the 25.000 refugees that you say congregated in and around the compound?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of those 25.000 refugees, most of them were women, children, and elderly people. I think, and that's what I stated before, there were about two to three per cent men between 16 and 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please describe the general conditions that were present in and around the compound.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The general conditions from the people, the refugees, it's what I explained before, was poorer than poor. They hadn't had food and water supplies during the six days of war over there. They were in very bad condition. We had no means to supply them, only by the water we had left into our own compound and some food and some medicines left. But the general condition of the people was miserable, more than miserable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Amongst those 25.000 refugees, were there some pregnant women who were delivering their babies?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. What I heard later on, there were five pregnant women with their little babies. What I heard was that one man hung himself during the stay over there. And life was, let's say, going on during the two days that we had all those refugees around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to turn your attention to air strikes. Can you please describe those air strikes to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. As everybody knows, I asked several times for air strikes, looking to the mandate, the mandate which asked in the beginning of the establishment of the safe areas of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, that one needed about 40.000 soldiers for that, and that was diminished after negotiations to about 8.000; that they changed the mandate in that sense, that they combined it with air strikes or, let's say, close air support, air support in general. That was one of the parts of the mandate and that was what I am referring to, that as soon as the attacks started on the 6th, I asked for close air support because one of the OPs was attacked, UN troops were attacked, the city of Srebrenica had been shelled. There was no close air support available on the days that I asked for that, except at the last day, on the 11th, on Tuesday. I asked that in the very early morning, I expected that at 6.00. I had a meeting during the night, from Monday to Tuesday, with the local authorities and the military authorities. We discussed that even, and I told them that we expected air strikes or close air support in the very early morning, on the 11th. That didn't come, didn't show up. After noon, about 2.00, the air strikes started. It had no effect on the population; it had no effect on the mission of the battalion because everybody knows that the air strikes or close air support was too late and too little. It had an effect on the way General Mladic reacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before I get to that point, let me just clarify one point with you, Colonel Karremans. It was your understanding when you were the commanding officer of the DutchBat unit in Srebrenica that air support was supposed to be a significant part of the protection measures available to you and to the population of Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned that there were air strikes and that they were too little, too late; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What effect did those air strikes have on General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effect was that through the hijacked soldiers, about 30 in Bratunac, on one of the BSA kazernes over there, Mladic or one of his officers used the communications equipment of the vehicles over there and ordered me to stop immediately using air support. And if that was not the case, if I wasn't able to stop that immediately, he should use all his weaponry, that's what he said, to shell the compound of Potocari, to shell the refugees within and around the compound, and kill the 30 hijacked soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did General Mladic have the ability to deliver on those threats?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could. He had the ability because he had gathered a lot of weaponry around the compound, on top of the hills, like mortars, two main bell tanks, artillery and, what I explained already yesterday, multiple rocket launch system from different types, all in direct sight or direct direction of the compound, and he could use that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In fact, he had already used that on the UN compound in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to another topic now, Colonel Karremans, and that is the meetings that you had with General Mladic. Can you explain the circumstances of your first meeting with General Mladic, and explain when it occurred and where is occurred.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The first meeting I had with General Mladic was on Tuesday night, at half past eight. I was notified by my ops room, they got a message, again through the same communications systems, that I had to show up in Bratunac for a meeting. I didn't know what kind of meeting that should be but I expected with somebody from the BSA, maybe Colonel Vukovic or Nikolic, or whatsoever. I wasn't before in Bratunac but my LO, liaison officers, had a couple of times been there talking about trade, about military options with the BSA, so they came with me, two liaison officers, and we went to the hotel in Bratunac. There was a crowd of military persons, all in combat wear, gear, and clothes. There I met for the first time General Mladic. I didn't know that he was there. I had not met him before, not in life. There was also General Zivanovic, the corps commander of the Drina Corps. We were all standing there at half past eight. There were a lot of press around, television, and General Mladic started accusing me of all things that happened in the last six days; that I was responsible for the air strikes or the air support, killed some of his people, soldiers; that my soldiers had tried to kill him because of shooting at him; that we were not able to disarm the BiH forces within the enclave, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When he was addressing you, was he speaking calmly?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was shouting more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we got our famous glass in our hands, water --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you describe how that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We just got a glass of something in our hand and didn't toast with that, but the circumstances were, if you can imagine, bad at that time because we too didn't sleep for five nights and had hardly no food, no water, lived in shelters and bunkers, so we were all, let's say, not well for a meeting like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there a camera crew present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a camera group present, and they put everything on tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After the glass was put in your hand, were pictures taken of you and other Dutch officers?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long did that meeting last, Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not too long. I think three-quarters of an hour. I was able to explain the poor situation of the refugees, which I did. I asked him for a supply of food, water, medicines, and then he said to me, "You will have to -- you should return for a second meeting at half past eleven, just before midnight," that I should take with me a representative of the refugees, if it was possible, one of the civil authorities of the opstina. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we went back to -- we left the hotel in Bratunac and drove back to the compound. The first thing I did there, I had a quick talk with my deputy battalion commander and we were desperately looking for a representative of the refugees. One of my officers knew, and he saw him, that the head or the director of the secondary school of Srebrenica was amongst the refugees, was in the compound of Potocari. We found him and we explained the situation, that I had had a meeting with General Mladic and that he ordered, more or less, me to bring with me to a second meeting one of the representatives -- a representative of the refugees. I asked him if he was willing to go with me to that meeting, and he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you then return to Bratunac that evening?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to Bratunac that evening, just before midnight, with my same two liaison officers and with Mr. Mandzic. Mr. Mandzic was the representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who were the representatives of the Bosnian Serb army at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less the same which I met in the first meeting: General Mladic, General Zivanovic; there was an interpreter which I referred already to yesterday, Mr. Petar, a couple of BSA officers, and one or two civilians who I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At that second meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can we stop here at this point for a break? There has to be something where you can end a phase. Is this a good end here now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll resume in half an hour, at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We're ready just to continue playing the tape of Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At that second meeting did you request permission for convoys to pass through and to ask permission for some form of relief of the refugees who were in and around your compound?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you please describe that second meeting.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second meeting was a little bit more friendlier than the first one, I must say, and I was able to explain again the very bad circumstances and the situation in and around the compound concerning the refugees. Again I asked for support on medicines, water supplies, food, the wounded. I had about 100 wounded persons in the field dressing station, all in shelters. He made note of my requests without saying if he could do something about it. Then he started with his demands in, let's say, a kind of monologue. He asked me, and also the representative of the refugees, Mr. Mandzic, that all Bosnian soldiers should lay down their weapons and deliver those weapons into the hands of the BSA. He said that he had a clear attitude towards the BiH soldiers: survive or disappear. He asked me and the representative to come back the next morning at 10.00 to have a third meeting. He promised that there would be a ceasefire, which I had asked for, until 10.00 the next morning, Wednesday, and if there won't be any support of the BiH in delivering their weapons, action should be taken by him by again shelling, what he stated before, of the compound and the refugees. He said something about Mr. Izetbegovic, the President of the Muslim people in Sarajevo, that he killed more Serb people during the last years than the Bosnian Serb army did. He stated that he was not willing to use power against women and children. He asked me if Naser Oric -- Naser Oric was, let's say, the commanding officer of the BiH forces -- if he could show up, I mean, if I could take him with me to the next meeting. I explained to him that we hadn't seen Naser Oric since April, he hadn't been back in the enclave since April. He stated that he was prepared to take over the about 100 or 110 wounded persons, and he guaranteed that if he had taken over -- should have taken over the wounded, he guaranteed that they would have the same treatment as what is normal for treating the wounded, according to the Conventions of Geneva, the Geneva Conventions. Again he stated or said or demanded that we should come back the next morning with a delegation of the people -- a delegation of the refugees, and if it was possible, these civilian and military authorities from the enclave. Again he stated that the handing over of the weapons by BiH soldiers would mean the survival of them. "If they should keep their weapons," he said, "that will be their death." He stated that if the BiH soldiers should hand over their weapons that they will be treated according to the Geneva Conventions. And he stated at the end that the destiny of the Muslim people was in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he also make any statement with regard to whether NATO or the UN were capable of guaranteeing the existence of the safe area?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He quoted some words on that subject, but that he already did in the first meeting. I'd like to say a "meeting," between brackets. He stated that the UN forces in general were not able to fulfil, let's say, the arrangements made by the ceasefire agreement and the UN resolutions as of 1993. I refer to the demilitarisation of the enclave. He said that in the first meeting and also in the second meeting, that "Your United Nations forces were not able to fulfil their mission."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, after that second meeting did you return to the UN compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We did return in the middle of the night. I think that meeting lasted one and a half hours in total. We went back to the compound of Potocari. I had a telephone call with sector north-east, told them what happened that day, what happened during those two meetings, what was demanded by General Mladic. Then we started looking for more representatives, to have them prepared for the meeting of the next morning. I had a long talk again with my deputy, with some officers of the battalion staff, how to find those specific persons, and at the end we found them. We found a woman and one other person. So I had, the next morning, three persons for the committee of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the next morning there was a third meeting, is that correct, Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third meeting took place again in Bratunac, in the same hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately what time did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was more or less as the second one. The same persons, at least most of them that I met in the second meeting, and there were some civilians as well who attended that meeting. I didn't know them. They were introduced but I can't remember which jobs they had. They were all from Bratunac and Zvornik. He started welcoming myself and the liaison officers, and also the committee of three persons --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "he," are you referring to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic, yes. Then the two other, let's say, the new representatives were able to introduce themselves shortly, starting with the woman. She made some statements, very clear statements, towards General Mladic about the very poor, bad, miserable circumstances of all the refugees, and that the refugees were not responsible for what happened in the enclave during the last two, three years, and that women and children were not responsible for those things which had been happening. She was the representative of all women and children. They were all civilians, and no military and no politicians. Also the man introduced himself and he asked for help, and he said, stated, not blaming the refugees, and that they need a lot of things which I have already stated -- had already stated before, like medicines, food, water, and other supplies. He said that neither he nor my battalion staff or myself were able to make contact with the Bosnian government during that night to ask for specific points for that third meeting, which meant that he wasn't able to lean on mandates or on other things to explain to General Mladic. After those statements of the two other representatives, and Mr. Mandzic was already invited to tell something about himself during the second meeting, the day before, General Mladic started his monologue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Will you describe that monologue, please.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very long monologue. He started with a piece of history, in 1992, that the Bosnian army, the Bosnian soldiers -- and he blamed Oric specially for that -- that they killed a lot of Bosnian Serb families, soldiers, civilians, that they attacked a lot of villages in the surroundings of the city of Srebrenica, devastated a lot of villages, and that according to that, what happened in 1993, as soon as those safe havens or safe areas had been established, that the destiny of poor people was in the hands of the Bosnian Serbs. That was one of his other statements, he said it was too late for help, help either by the Bosnian government or by the UN troops. He said that there was a lot of misery in the last years, that the BiH forces within the enclave had murdered a lot around the enclave by raids looking for food, revenge, looking for revenge, terror. He stated that he was willing to assist the refugees, those 25.000 refugees, but that he needed assistance, assistance by the local civilian and military authorities, from which I already explained that they were not available at the moment, not within that group of 25.000 refugees. He again said regarding the BiH forces, the same expression as the day before, survive or disappear. He again requested to the BiH forces to hand over their weapons. Even criminals amongst them could hand over their weapons. The second subject he stated was that the gathered population in and around the compound had the choice either to stay in Srebrenica or to be evacuated, to be evacuated to Serbia, toward the Bosnian territory around Tuzla, or even to foreign countries. He said that the whole former -- at that moment, former safe area had been encircled by his forces and that fighting should stop. We could hear that during the night before, and the day, that there were still fights and attacks going on. He stated that he was not able to assist the refugees as long as fighting was going on. He stated that the BiH forces could hand over their weapons in the presence of UN forces; UNPROFOR, he stated in general. I think he meant DutchBat. He stated that he was willing to assist with the evacuation. That was the first time, in the third meeting, that he used the word "evacuation." Then he stated that there used to be a good life in and around Srebrenica and in around the vicinity of Srebrenica, and that he liked to have the same situation, that good life before 1992, and that he'd like to have that situation back. He said that looking back, or referring to that lecture in history, that he didn't like to kill, what happened in 1992 and 1993, and he, as a professional soldier, had no joy in killing either civilians or military. Again he offered his help, and the committee of refugees should think that over, think about how they could assist in the evacuation. He asked for basic needs, I mean, what did we use -- what did the refugees use concerning food, water, medicines, medical support, and so forth. He asked again how many refugees there were and we answered again 25.000, around 25.000. The committee stated that most of the refugees liked to go to their family and be gathered together with their husbands, and he stated that nobody should be forced to be evacuated. On the other hand, he said that if NATO air strikes or air support should be the case in other areas in Bosnia, that he should use his weaponry again and taking sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you explain what he meant by that.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same what he said or stated in the first meeting, before the first meeting, that if air strikes should occur again, that he should shell, let's say, the compound and the refugees in and around the compound. He said that he would like to see all the men between 17 and 60, and I asked him, and also both men in the delegation, "What for?" and his answer was that he'd like to see all those persons because he said, he stated, that there were a lot of war criminals amongst them and he would like to speak with them. Again he asked if we were able to come in contact with soldiers whom Mladic knew. He was referring, of course, to Naser Oric, which I explained to him before that he was not available, and some other persons, let's say, the commanding officers of the BiH within the enclave. Again I told him that there were no BiH soldiers available at the moment. So there was no possibility to look for them because we were gathered together with all the refugees in a very, very small area, I mean, the compound and the two or three factories just in the vicinity of it. And we lost our eyes and ears in the rest of the enclave so we were not able to pick up those military representatives. Then he stated in his monologue that the BiH soldiers had only 24 hours to hand over all the weapons. After that statement, he asked some very specific conditions of the refugees, and he stated that if he was able to assist, he preferred in a kind of priority to look for the weak persons first, for the wounded persons, and later on the rest of the refugees, women and children. He said that nobody should be hurt and that coordination and cooperation with UNPROFOR, DutchBat in particular, was one of his priorities. What I just stated, that he mentioned "evacuation" during his monologue for the first time, he asked for diesel for the evacuation. You can imagine that I started laughing a little bit because he was exactly aware of what I had for diesel, that there was none, nothing, nil, and that I was not able to support him by giving him diesel. He said that his forces, BSA forces, will give escort during the evacuation. I said, "No. If there should be an evacuation anyway, that my own battalion should escort the evacuation." Then I explained to him in which way I should execute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was your proposal to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My proposal was to put on every vehicle one soldier, not knowing how many vehicles there were. As soon as the evacuation started the same day, at 3.00, I think we'll come to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll come to that a little later in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was unable to do that, I was unable to put on each vehicle one soldier. Then he said, and it was quite a remarkable expression, that Allah won't help, was not able to help, and Mladic could. He gave his word. He said to the commission not to be in panic, not to be afraid, and asked them to send that message to the refugees. I asked again when that was possible what happened or what should happen with the men between 17 and 60, and he again said or stated that there were quite some war criminals amongst them and that he liked to investigate, person by person, what they have done and what kind of persons those were. At the end of that meeting, all of a sudden he started to tell something about the evacuation again, and he proposed, let's say it in that way, "proposed," that Kladanj should be the point for evacuation. Kladanj is a small village just on the border between Bosnian Serb territory and the Bosnian territory around Tuzla. In fact, Kladanj is the first Muslim city in that area. He repeated that within 24 hours all soldiers of the BiH, even in uniform or not in uniform, even war criminals amongst the BiH forces, could hand over and should hand over the weapons. He said, "It's better to live than to die." Then he referred to something, what I said already yesterday or explained yesterday, that he knew everything that was going on in the enclave, what happened in the enclave day by day, and that he had persons in the enclave who informed him every day. So he was well aware of what was going on. Then he showed to us at the end of the meeting a book, that was a book of the opstina, a book in which marriages were assigned by people, marriage, and that the last marriage was on the 29th of June. He had as a piece of remembrance, I presume, a thing from, let's say, the entry of the opstina. He ended with something to say to the woman of the committee, that she was a fine woman, that she was open, or had been open in the way of statements towards Mladic, and he didn't say anything to both male representatives. Last but not least, he asked us, urged us, in finding a contact with the BiH forces and to convince them to hand over their weapons within 24 hours. That was, I think, the whole meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What time did the meeting end, Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about noonish, about 12.00, because at 12.30 I had a meeting in the compound with the committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What time did the first transports arrive to take the refugees away from the compound?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said during the third meeting, I forgot to say that, that the evacuation should start about 1.00. But it wasn't well-organised in the beginning, or efficiently organised, so the evacuation started at 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So three hours from the conclusion of your meeting with General Mladic transport arrived in and around Potocari to start taking the refugees away.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What type of transport arrived?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of buses, I think 20 or 30, vans, big lorries, and small military vehicles. I think the first evacuation was about between 40 and 50 vehicles, and that was also, let's say, one of my decision points to change from one soldier at every vehicle to what we had done later on, put two vehicles with officers to escort the evacuations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So as a result of the number of vehicles, you realised that you did not have enough troops to put on one soldier per vehicle to accompany the convoy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So did you formulate another solution?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We formulated, indeed, another solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Describe that solution, please.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That solution was that we should escort each convoy by two vehicles, two jeeps, Mercedes jeeps; in every jeep, one officer or non-commissioned officer and a driver with communications, up to Kladanj, and then they should return and pick up, let's say, the next evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened to those escort vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first escort or in the first evacuation, I put my personnel officer, a captain, and one of the liaison officers, and they managed to go with all the persons in that convoy to cross the border in the area of Kladanj. The vehicles that left in the convoy returning to Srebrenica disappeared, and that happened with the other vehicles during the next evacuations too. And totally, or in total, 14, they were just picked up en route by -- either by BSA forces or irregular forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
