utterances.text: So I understand clearly, the first escort vehicle made it to Kladanj, is that correct, or made it to a point shortly --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six kilometres --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: From Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from Kladanj, because there was a barricade between the two borders and that meant that all the refugees, and later on also wounded persons, were forced to walk, struggle, I must say, the last six kilometres to the border of Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did any other of your escort vehicles make it to Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them in the beginning --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but they didn't return.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So what happened to those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were hijacked, stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened to the equipment that was used by the soldiers who participated in those escorts?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same. Weaponry, their personal weapons were stolen. Helmets, flak jackets, private belongings were stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the consequence of losing those vehicles in relation to the convoys that left your compound?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consequences were, I think, threefold. In the first place, again we changed the way of escorting those convoys by putting en route, and the route was about 50 kilometres, four different points, let's say, contact points, so that the vehicles standing there on fixed points could see convoys passing, counting the amount of vehicles. What we did in the beginning, as soon as a convoy left, let's say, the road in front of the compound, we counted the amount of vehicles and gave that to the first fixed post so that they could have a look and control if the same amount of vehicles were still in that convoy. The second thing we did is that I ordered troops just outside the compound to work either in groups, armed, with their helmets and flak jackets, or if they work individually, like the soldiers, the doctors, et cetera, that they should work just in a T-shirt, without a helmet, without a flak jacket, and without a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in the beginning, especially for individuals working between the refugees, they have been stolen from the BSA soldiers around, there were not so many. They stole the helmets, personal weapons, and flak jackets just by pointing a weapon on the head of the soldier and said, "I'd like to have it. Give it to me." They didn't do that when groups were working outside, then they didn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you again see General Mladic on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on Wednesday, yes. At the moment that the first convoy arrived, let's say, the empty vehicles, and turned around in front of the compound and the first refugees were escorted to all those buses, vans, and military vehicles, General Mladic appeared with his own vehicle and all his officers around him, and some bodyguards of course. And the press was there available too; they made nice pictures of him and what was going on over there. A lot of publicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations with General Mladic on this fourth meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a short conversation with him about the evacuation, about what he stated in the morning, that first priority should be the wounded persons, which he stated, "Yes, that's correct, we should do something about it. Bring them over to the hospital in Bratunac." Then I said, "No, we won't do that. They will stay here in the compound, in our own hands, or they should be sent or brought to NorMed Corps," that's the Norwegian Medical Company in Tuzla, "escorted by either the Norwegian Company or by the International Red Cross."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please continue your description of the fourth meeting with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was so busy during his stay there with the press and impressing his soldiers and the officers around him, and talking to some refugees, that I had hardly any chance to talk with him longer than, I think, those five minutes, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was your next contact with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next contact was the next morning, on Thursday, Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again in front of the compound, just opposite the gate, the main gate. Again, a short meeting. There was no press available, or present, I must say. He had only Colonel Jankovic with him and Major Nikolic, both officers of the BSA, and of course his interpreter, Petar, and some bodyguards. He offered me, that was on that Thursday morning, he offered me that we could go or leave the compound with vehicles after or during the evacuation of all the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In other words, that the Dutch Battalion could evacuate --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was your response?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that I didn't like the idea of leaving the compound because of a couple of subjects. One of the subjects was that I still had some military on OP Alpha, one of the observation posts that was still occupied. The officers and the soldiers from the day before, escorting the convoys that were still under way, I missed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In other words, they were still missing.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were still missing. I was faced at that moment with 55 wounded civilians within the compound, and I referred to the talk we had before, that I'd like to bring them over either by NorMed Coy or by the International Red Cross; that I had my Bosnian local workers on the compound, I mean, interpreters from the battalion, interpreters from the United Nations Military Observers which I had on the compound; that I had all the people of the MSF, Medecins Sans Frontiers, with me on the compound, and that if we leave, we leave all together but after some arrangements concerning the wounded persons had been made. That was my answer. He agreed with that and that's why I stayed in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there any other significant matters discussed at that meeting, or did that conclude the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That concluded the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: By the end of the 13th of July, had all the refugees been deported from the Potocari compound area?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I will look at my notebook. At 1600, on Thursday, the last refugee was gone outside the compound, and then one started with the evacuation of the 4.000 to 5.000 refugees which were able to stay within the compound. It started at 1600 and it finished about 7.00. That was in three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the end of that -- at 7.00, then, there were no further refugees in and around Potocari; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no further refugees in and around Srebrenica -- I mean the compound at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was the next time you saw General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next time that I saw General Mladic was on the day of our departure, on the 21st of July. It was on a Friday morning. We had eight days to prepare our own, let's say, departure, to rest. On Friday, the day after the evacuation, all of a sudden a convoy with food, a lot of food, a lot of diesel, was accepted and came to the Potocari area. So then we had -- from that day we had enough food, enough diesel, medicines, and we had eight days to recover from what happened in the weeks before. I saw General Mladic on a Friday. He invited me through, I think it was, Colonel Jankovic who came to the compound that morning, on Friday morning, or Petar, the interpreter, he said that I was invited with my liaison officers to that same hotel in Bratunac where I had my three meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We drove to that hotel in one vehicle with my liaison officers. There was General Mladic with a crowd of officers; most of them I knew already from the meetings. My own -- well, that's not the right expression. The chief of staff of the BH command, General Nicolae, was there, a Dutch General, and his military assistant and they offered us breakfast, and we had some talks over a couple of things, about weaponry. I asked him again what happened with my weaponry and that I'd like to have it back. I knew already that we should leave at noon towards the Serbian territory, and then the way up to Zagreb. Again I asked, "Where are all my vehicles? I'd like to have them back with me." Then he said, after some general things but I have forgotten those, that he'd like to visit the compound, look to our own convoys, how we did that, the vehicles. He asked me to have a talk with the soldiers and that that should occur at 11.00, whether that was possible in the time frame. It was not possible. So I told General Mladic that it wasn't such a good idea, talking to soldiers, not such a good idea, visiting the compound, but he insisted on visiting the compound. He said, "Okay. I won't be there at 11.00. I will be there, escorted by the chief of staff of the BH command, at 11.30." I left the hotel. We went back to the compound of Potocari. I had a quick talk with my deputy, seeing that everything was arranged for our own travel with everything which had been left. That was the case. I asked my deputy, "Are we able to start at noon?" He said yes, he could. I told him that General Mladic would come. He said okay. We went back to the gate and he was already there before half past eleven. He was held up by the commander of the guard, a very broad sergeant. He couldn't go around that Sergeant. He was held up. General Mladic had a quick talk with him, and then it was half past eleven. I took him with me to my own briefing room within the compound, had a quick talk -- I think 20 minutes -- about some general things. Then I asked him two specific questions. One question was, "What will happen with my equipment?" I told him what equipment I lost during the last two weeks: all my field vehicles, the armoured personnel carriers, a lot of personal arms, machine-guns, the equipment of most of the observation posts. That was the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was his response?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: His response was that he should sort that out. He was in contact with his Ministry of Internal Affairs, and they should do that in close combination or coordination, I must say, with the BH command. He referred to the presence of the chief of staff of BH command. My second question which I can remember asking him was just a general one. I asked him what should happen or should have happened if, during the stay of the United Nations troops in the safe areas of Gorazde, Zepa, and especially, of course, Srebrenica, what would happen if BH soldiers were disarmed totally, completely demilitarised, if they shouldn't have executed raids outside the compound -- outside the enclave, if both civilian and military authorities should live according to the 1993 regulations, arrangements, and ceasefire regulations, then he answered that he -- at least that was his answer -- would not have thought about attacking the enclave. He said it with a smile more or less, and that was also more or less the end of our discussion there in the briefing room. Then we went outside to the entry of the compound, gate, main gate of the compound. The guards were changed. My guards went back to their company. Everybody in their vehicles, and exactly at noon we started leaving the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, thank you very much. I have no further questions. Your Honours, I have concluded my examination of Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Let me look at fellow Judges. Judge Odio-Benito, I do believe you have some questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, after leaving Srebrenica and Potocari, where did the refugees go in these convoys, buses and trucks, you have explained?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, all refugees, which I explained, left the safe area of Srebrenica within an amazingly short time -- that was Wednesday afternoon and Thursday, the whole day -- and they had been evacuated to the Kladanj area, the one -- the first, let's say, Muslim city in the Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: To the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the confrontation line, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to them during the travel?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because they stayed in vehicles. That was one of the things that I'd like to do in the beginning, to put a soldier per vehicle to have a look what was going on in buses or trucks. They didn't inform me what was going on in the buses because we didn't have eyes and ears for that. The only thing we could do, and that was the second option, was just escorting those big groups of vehicles, convoys, by two cars, in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: But your vehicles and cars were stolen by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: What did your soldiers do after that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the soldiers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Yes, because you had soldiers in those vehicles and they lost the vehicles, the helmets, everything. But what did they do?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were gathered together during that night, the night of Wednesday and Thursday, by the Bosnian Serb army, or the irregular part of it, I don't know exactly. They were gathered together, I think 12 in total, or 14 officers and soldiers. They stayed overnight two times. Somewhere along that route, the route from Bratunac to Kladanj, they were fed by the Bosnian Serb army. They could have shelter for their own protection, they said. On Friday they returned, through Bratunac, to my compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Did you or any of your soldiers see Bosnian Serb soldiers beating, killing, raping the refugees in or around Potocari, in those factories that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they did. In some cases refugees had been beaten, and as soon as one of my soldiers noticed that, they stopped with it. I got two reports from my soldiers on Thursday, after I met General Mladic; one report referring to an execution of one man and a second report about an execution of nine men of which they found the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will be presenting evidence in regard to both of those incidents described by Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever ask General Mladic during your meetings what happened to the people, the refugees?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the last meeting I had with him was on the 21st, that was eight days later on, and we were not aware of what happened with the refugees. I mean, in general, I know -- I knew that they were all evacuated to the Kladanj area and afterwards picked up by the Pakistani Battalion and by the International Red Cross, by the Norwegian Medical Company. They built tents, shelters, supply points for the refugees. A part of them had been transported to the air base of Tuzla and other parts of the amount of refugees were transported to other facilities. That's the only thing I knew, and I didn't discuss that with General Mladic at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Would you say, Colonel, that you received adequate support you asked for from your superiors?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: During those difficult days before the fall of Srebrenica, you told us that you asked for support.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Did you receive that support?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can expand on that for days and days, of course. That's why I was lucky that I could explain yesterday and at the beginning of the morning what happened with the inhabitants in the enclave, the refugees, and with my soldiers. We had our daily sitreps, our daily situation reports, in which we wrote everything that happened that day, what we needed for supplies. Besides that, I reported at different times, several times, I must say, on the level of north-east command in Tuzla and the BH command in Sarajevo, what I needed to fulfil my mission. I was very specific in that, exactly what we needed, medicines, food, diesel, et cetera. I asked for support many, many times during our stay over there. I know that there have been many discussions on all levels, above the level of the battalion, sitting there with the population, isolated in an enclave like Srebrenica, but we didn't get any support at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a last question and ask for your personal opinion, Colonel. Looking back, would you say that the United Nations and NATO did its best to help people, to save their lives?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the one hand, yes. If we should have had our freedom of movement, which was one of the points of the NATO -- United Nations resolutions of 1993, and we could travel back and forth to the safe areas in general, and to Srebrenica in particular, for my battalion but also for the International Red Cross, the other non-governmental organisations like the MSF, the UNHCR, and we were able to assist, help, the refugees, I think the answer is yes. But because of the strangulation and because of the isolation and not having had support at all, then the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Strangulation and isolation ordered by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I now ask my other fellow Judge if he has any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, throughout these, perhaps, five meetings that you had with General Mladic, did he ever take into consideration your demands, or was it always, as you said, a monologue and he did not respond to any of your objections or claims?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have had, let's say, three major meetings with him, but "meetings" between brackets, because in my opinion, a meeting is two directions and a monologue is not a meeting. Indeed, those were monologues. In the second meeting I was able to explain the bad situation, and he made even notes of that, and that was it. The third meeting, on Wednesday morning, the woman and the other men of the committee could make their statements. They made note of it and that was it. So the conclusion, only monologues, no two-way negotiations. He did listen to my requests, if I may say so, but didn't support them at all. He had his own line in negotiating or in telling what he would like to tell and what he'd like to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you express any disapproval of his method of separating men, as you said, between 16 and, I think, 60 or 65 from women and children? Did you object to that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour. I objected to that already in the meeting when he said that by asking, "What is the meaning of that?" His explanation was what I stated before, that he'd like to have the men between 16 and 60, to look if there were war criminals amongst them. Maybe he thought that all the Bosnian soldiers were war criminals. He didn't explain what he'd like to do with them except that he wants to speak with them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did he ask you for information about these people, to give him any kind of indication of where they are and who they are?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So there was absolutely no way of knowing about them through your battalion.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In your last meeting with him, you said it was on Friday morning, by that time it seems that you had already known about the executions you mentioned. Were you aware of everything that had happened and the way the refugees fleeing away were treated?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think not at all. The information in those days confirmed the information about, let's say, the military side of what was going on in the battalion, resupplying, what had to be done before our own evacuation, if I may say so, and lastly, what happened during our week that we stayed there, and negotiations between some of the officers of my battalion staff and some of the BSA soldiers on wounded persons. I had still one of the colonel surgeons in Bratunac in hospital to see what was going on with the wounded persons over there. We had discussions about the diesel because on that Friday after the evacuations I got a lot of diesel; what we should do with medicines and food. Those were more or less the subjects we discussed in a couple of, let's say, small meetings, not with General Mladic, because I haven't seen him after the evacuation, but with his officers. I think that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But did you include any mention, not to say protest, against the executions or the things you heard about in this last meeting you had with him, and what was his response, if you did?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't protested in the last meeting because I even didn't expect that meeting. I was not aware of that because we came -- we had a message through our communications systems, the ops room, then had to show up, let's put it that way, again in the Bratunac Hotel. Sitting with his whole crowd over there, we had -- he was again a lit bit monologueing and asking me how the battalion was, how they were doing, and if we were prepared to move and ready to go, and there was hardly any opportunity to evaluate, let's put it that way, what happened in all the weeks and days before. To be frank, I hadn't thought about the idea of asking him what happened with the refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: According to you, he was present all the time and he was aware of all that was happening.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was present during the six days there of the attack and invasion of the enclave, at least I presume. He was present during the evacuation. He had been there two times, which I explained, and if he wasn't there, he was at the hotel in Bratunac which he used as a command post, and a kazerne in Bratunac which he used as a command post for, let's say, the other things he had to do concerning Gorazde, Zepa, and I don't know what. After my last meeting with him, a short, short meeting on that Thursday morning, I hadn't seen him before -- I hadn't seen him afterwards, except that I got some orders from the higher echelons about our own travel to either the Kladanj/Tuzla area or to Zagreb -- that was still a point of discussion on the higher echelons -- and one asked me if I could, let's say, come in contact with General Mladic to discuss that, because nobody had contact with him since the evacuation, nobody from the higher commands. So I got, let's say, some notes by fax, made a small letter about it and sent that to his interpreter, Petar, who lived in Bratunac, with the request to hand it over to General Mladic and ask for a response. I got a response, I think, on Friday, the same Friday when the first convoys with food and diesel came in. That was the only contact on paper I had with him. In his reply, or his answer, he said, "Yes, I will take your requests concerning your leave, whenever that should occur, and your requests on the lost equipment," he said "lost equipment," not "stolen equipment," he will take that into consideration and asked me to have patience. He should have a meeting with General Smith on Sunday, and I think that occurred on the 19th, and in that meeting he should discuss the leave of DutchBat, and then he should come back to, let's say, make all the arrangements for our leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You speak of evacuation, and you mentioned that several times he asked you to assist in this evacuation; that means, really, that the deportation of the people of Srebrenica to the Bosniak side. This deportation, although you did not assist, was very highly organised, and you said that buses came and that everything was very minutely organised. So this was the headquarters of Mladic who did it.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was -- I think he ordered that himself. What I stated before during many briefings, also open that everything was prepared -- preplanned in advance. And also the massive crowd of buses and vehicles, and I always use the example, in modern Western countries, if you like to have 30 or 40 buses, then you have a challenge, but in a country like the former Yugoslavia or Bosnia-Herzegovina, to gather there 30 or 40 buses, you are not able to do that in one day, that must be preplanned a long time before. So he had a plan and he executed that plan more or less minute by minute or day by day. He ordered for the evacuation. He asked for assistance of the battalion but not more than -- and you will hear that from the next, I think, witnesses -- assist the people to go to the bus, prevail -- prevent, I must say, panic, chaos, and supplying the refugees, as much as I could, with water, food, and medicines, at least what I have left over. That was the only assistance I could give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that 55 soldiers were taken into custody by the Serbs. I think it was on the 6th of July. How were they treated and how long did they stay?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was not on the 6th of July. On the 6th of July, on the Thursday, let's say, the invasions started, the attacks or -- yes, the attacks started, the fighting between both parties in the southern part of the enclave, also by shelling compounds and the city of Srebrenica itself. It ended up on Saturday, two and a half days later, on the retreat of OP Foxtrot that one of my soldiers died. After that, let's say, Saturday afternoon and Sunday and Monday, he picked -- or he attacked a lot of observation posts by using force, weapons and soldiers, encircled them -- circled them and took the soldiers hostage and took them with him. He gathered at the end 55 of my soldiers at two points; one in Bratunac, in the northern part of -- let's say north of the enclave, and one in Simici, south of the enclave. At the end, after the evacuation, they were gathered together, all 55. I had a talk with them, not with all 55 but with 30 persons staying in Bratunac, and I asked, in the first meeting I had with General Mladic, if I was able or allowed to speak with them. "Yes," he said, "you are able to do that, you are allowed to do that." I had a small talk with the soldiers, asked them if they were treated well. They said yes, they were treated reasonably well. And that same applied, which I heard later on already being back in the Netherlands, to the other 25 soldiers from Simici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned several times that you raised the matter to the higher echelons, to your higher echelons. Was there a prompt response, or did they leave you just to your fate?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the circumstances at that time and knowing that both commanding officers of the north-east command and the BH command were not available, I had to deal with both chiefs of staff. My direct superior was, of course, the commanding officer of north-east command in Tuzla. What I did was every time I thought it was necessary, in shelters and in my own offices or in the communication centre of the battalion staff, I had direct communications with either the north-east command or BH command. We did report -- we did make our reports verbally, at least I did it -- it was one of my responsibilities to the higher echelons -- and we did it every day at 6.00 by the daily situation reports, on paper, by fax. In conclusion, my direct superior in Tuzla, but also the command in Sarajevo, were well aware of what was going on and what happened minute by minute in the enclave, every day of our stay over there. Again, asking for support, logistical support, in the weeks before, or even, which I stated before, close air support, no. The support was words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you also, in one of the meetings where you mentioned Major Nikolic, he stated that all Muslims should leave Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That was at an official meeting?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- no. We had a sequence of meetings with both parties, not together. We tried to have them together around the negotiation table. My predecessor did. He wasn't able to do that one or two times. We weren't because of the quarrels, because of the fights over and over. So we had, every week, a fixed meeting with the civil authorities, with the military authorities, within the enclave, and also with, let's say, the commanding officer of the chief of staff of the BiH forces. We should have a meeting, a fixed meeting, every two weeks with the BSA outside, either on OP Echo or OP Papa, but that was not the case. Meetings with the BSA were always when we liked to have that or when they liked to have it, very irregularly. It was at one of those irregular meetings where I was involved, somewhere in the middle of February, if I can remember, that I met Major Nikolic, and it was at that meeting that he stated what I said yesterday, about the Muslims killed half the Assembly during the Second World War, et cetera, and that he hated Muslims and, in his opinion, the Muslims should leave the complete territory of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have some very short questions I would like to put to you. The troops you talked about, where did they come from? What was their composition? You talked about the fresh troops that arrived.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We were -- no. Around the safe area of Srebrenica there were three brigades: the so-called Skelani Brigade in the south, the Bratunac Brigade in the north, and a third brigade in the west. Those brigades belonged to the regular army of the BSA, the regular Drina Corps. But those three brigades consisted of elderly soldiers, soldiers from that area, an area where they belonged. As soon as -- on the 6th of July the invasion started or, let's say, the attack of the enclave started, which General Mladic stated later on he used three new brigades, one in the south, one in the east, and he had one in reserve in the north. That means that he didn't use the regular forces around the safe area of Srebrenica. He especially used other forces, which we had noticed two days before the 6th of July. In Bratunac there was a lot of battle noise, there was a lot of noise in moving tanks, artillery, military vehicles, all those moves which we had reported on on a regular basis and in our daily sitreps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Did you think there were any militia, fresh people, fresh militia, in these forces?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, what I had heard, I hadn't noticed that myself, was that the so-called Arkan's Brigade was involved as well. That was a brigade with, let's say, special forces from the BSA. But personally I didn't see them during those six days and during, let's say, the evacuation of refugees. That could be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The evacuation with the Dutch Battalion, was it possibly in the plan with your superior? Was the Dutch Battalion asked to provide that assistance?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the assistance, Your Honour, for the evacuation of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the evacuation. You've talked about a meeting with General Mladic, I think it was the second or the third, I can't remember, where all of a sudden he said that you had to proceed with the evacuation. It seems that it wasn't tackled during your first or second meeting in Bratunac. So I had the impression that you weren't surprised, that you knew that there might be an evacuation, or did you decide, as the superior, did you decide that the evacuation would take place?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first two meetings I didn't have a clue about what was going on about the destiny of the refugees. Knowing that we had about 25.000 refugees in and around the compound, one of my major points was to ask support, as much as I could get, from the BSA; what I stated before, food, water medicines, a good arrangement for my wounded -- for the wounded refugees, about 100 or 110, and that is what I asked for during the meetings -- the first meetings with General Mladic. In his third meeting he started to talk about evacuation, and that was a surprise for me as well. We arranged a committee of the refugees to cooperate with them about what should be done, or what should we do on the circumstances under which those refugees were there in and around our compound, what could we do, as much as possible, and we needed a committee for that, to talk about it. I used that committee -- and I mean in a nice sense of using it -- I asked them if they could assist me as much as possible, at least to respond to the questions, and they, that committee, went with me to the third meeting. That was the meeting where General Mladic stated or told about the evacuation. I was as surprised as everybody was, because the meeting was at the end of Wednesday morning and at 3.00 Wednesday afternoon the evacuation started already. So I was confronted with something new, an evacuation of 25.000 persons, and then I have to think quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I'm sorry. I heard what you said but what I'm trying to find out is: Faced with that surprise -- you were surprised, you said; the refugee committee was surprised -- did you have adequate time to ask your hierarchial structure to see whether you can proceed in such a way, or did you have sufficient freedom to decide?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no time to -- I had time to inform my higher echelons, which I did. I asked several times what could I do, how could you assist me, what should I do. No answer on that. There was no policy in that either. So I could, let's say, do what was the best thing to do at the moment. And knowing what time was left between that third meeting and 1.00, which was mentioned by Mladic when the evacuation should start -- we were completely surprised, everybody, that such a thing could happen and that he already had organised such an evacuation -- I wasn't able to do anything about it. That's why we decided -- I decided in the beginning to put on every bus, or whatsoever, a soldier, that was the least I could do, and assist the refugees as much as possible in going to the buses, giving them food, water, and medical care, and look for them during the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My final question. If you talk about the list -- we talked yesterday to the investigator from the Prosecution, and it seems that there was a list of men in an age range which I did not quite understand. Can you very quickly tell us what happened with this list of men? What was their age and what happened?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had, as you know, Your Honour, 25.000 persons in and around the enclave, almost all women, children, and elderly people. We estimated about two to three per cent men, men between 16 and 60 more or less, and we didn't know how many men there were -- in general we knew -- how many men there were outside the compound. We had asked through the interpreters and through the committee if it was possible to note or, yes, set on a piece of paper all the names of those persons, male persons, between 16 and 60 within the compound. There was no time left to do that for all the other persons. There was one person who asked me in the past, "Why didn't you put the names of all the refugees on a piece of paper?" You can imagine, Your Honours, that that's impossible. What we did was we put the names of men within the compound on a list, what I can remember, 239. There were about 70 who didn't like that and they didn't do that. We have done that on purpose because we would like to know what could have happened with those persons. What happened with the list, the lists have been faxed to Tuzla and to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Colonel, the Tribunal would like to thank you for your testimony. Last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Colonel, did by any chance General Mladic's office get hold of this list?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the answer I should give now, because there are two possible answers and maybe one of the witnesses after me could answer that question. There are two possible answers. One said, or it has been stated that one of my officers offered or handed over that list to one of the BSA officers at the gate. Some others said, no, that was not the case. I am still at this moment not aware of what was going on with the list towards the BSA. I don't know. I can't answer the question, do or does the BSA -- did the BSA receive that list of persons. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you ask the officer?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, based on the numerous questions we put -- once again, thank you, Colonel Karremans, to have spent so much time with us -- but do you have any wish to add any supplementary questions or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Colonel, in this Mladic/Karadzic case, we have finished with your testimony, and we will now finish until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think it's time for us to have a break. [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Olivier Fourmy has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think I would like to make a general remark at this point with regard to the French transcript of the testimony of Colonel Karremans and with regard to the Rule 61 hearing. I think that it contains a certain number of mistakes with regard to the substance that was stated, at least in the French version. I think that when Colonel Karremans speaks about BH command in English, he was talking about the one in Sarajevo not the Bosnian army which changes the sense of what he was saying. Perhaps the Prosecutor could confirm this, what I have just put forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Mark Harmon ought to respond to that, perhaps. [In English] What do you think, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As we saw, he was there and would probably be in a good position to respond. But I don't doubt Mr. Fourmy's statement. I'm sure there are some errors that might change things a little bit; that just seems to be a natural part of the process. But we can discuss that with Mr. Harmon and see if we need to make a change or try to add an addendum or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We'll trust you with this mission. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fourmy, for that important correction. [In English] I suggest we have a break for half an hour, and then we'll try to finish with your videos today, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have another video of Mr. Koster that lasts for 59 minutes so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. If we start at 1.35, 1.40, will we finish by 2.40?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll be a little over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'll request our interpreters and our staff to give us ten minutes more. Thank you. The hearing is adjourned for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may. I do apologise. But in this case, if we were to continue working late, we're going to have the same problem we had yesterday with the medical intervention for General Krstic, medical treatment, so we have the same problem. We should like to propose -- the Defence proposes, if you permit, that General Krstic could leave the courtroom earlier, like he did yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The same solution would apply today too. He can either leave now or he can leave at 2.15, it's up to him. But you agree that we should finish with the videos today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The trial is adjourned for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We're ready to go with the testimony of Mr. Koster, which is 59 minutes. We have another tape which we'll save for another time of Pasaga Mesic, which is about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Which means that we have another hour and a half to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, for two witnesses. One witness is an hour and then the other witness is 30 minutes, but we can save that for a time -- if there's ever a time we don't have enough witnesses in the trial, we can put in that tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm ready for both options, so what do you prefer? What does the Defence counsel prefer, and the registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've talked about it and the one-hour tape appears to be, with Mr. Harmon's input, the decision that we've made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. So one hour will take us to ten to three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That will be enough, I think. We'll stop at ten to three, with the permission of the interpreters. If there is any objection, I'm ready to hear it, if anybody has a commitment which he cannot avoid. So everybody agrees. Of course, General Krstic will be allowed to leave at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should just like to ask you so as not to lose time whether, without your permission at that stage, General Krstic can leave at 2.15, in the presence of the security officers, of course. May he leave the courtroom at that time, without me having to ask you again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You don't need to ask me. Thank you. The permission is granted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We would like to call our next witness, Lieutenant Koster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant Koster, do you hear me? Do you hear me? Please take the statement which has been given to you and read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Lieutenant. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think my first question would go to the Prosecutor, and he will introduce you to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Lieutenant Koster, would you please state your full name and spell it for the record.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: My last name is Koster. I'll spell it. K-o-s-t-e-r.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: I'm a logistics officer and an infantry soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: In the Dutch army?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: In the Dutch army, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Have you been serving with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Court where and when?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: I served in Srebrenica, and that was January 1995 till July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When did you start, did you say?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: In January.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: In January. Was Colonel Karremans your commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What was your position with the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: My position was to be the logistics officer of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Just give us the outline of your duties in that position.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, I had to manage all logistic affairs, although we had few means, and, well, that meant very strict planning and distributing our logistic affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Where in the chain of command were you placed in that position?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: I was a staff officer, and my direct commander, my logistic commander, was Major Franken.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you on duty in the beginning of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: I was on duty in Potocari, inside the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Inside the compound.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So your working place was inside the compound mostly.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Most of the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Okay. You were there even on the 11th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I was also outside the compound then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Will you tell us about what happened after the fall of Srebrenica when refugees started to arrive in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, that was on the 12th -- sorry, that was on the 11th of July. We were ordered to go outside and to form a unit to receive the refugees. So we went outside and made a hole in the fence from where we could guide the refugees towards the compound. When we were posted outside, approximately at 1500 hours, the refugees arrived in a few and small groups at first, and, well, most of them were women and children and older women and older men. They were terrified, they were afraid, looking for help, and when we were there, well, we couldn't tell them what to do at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You said that you formed a unit to take care of the incoming refugees. How big was that unit?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, approximately 30 men at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Were you in command of these 30 men?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You said you opened a hole in the fence.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Is that the way you led them into the compound?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. We were not allowed to let them in by the main gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Because the road which led from Srebrenica to Potocari was constantly under the direct sight and direct fire from the Serbs. For example, in the days before when we left the compound by vehicle, we were fired upon with mortar fire, that kind of thing. So it was better for people to take another route and another way to the compound which was more covered by trees and buildings. So that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: And you opened that hole in the fence.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When the people started to arrive, the first ones who arrived, did you show them all into the compound?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: No, we were not allowed at first. We first showed them the way to the large buildings of a former bus station, where bus repair and bus maintenance was done, and we told them to take cover inside of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When you are saying that you were not allowed, allowed by whom?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: By my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: By your commander.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What was the kind of shelter you gave them?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What kind of shelter did you give them?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: The big buildings of the former bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Outside the compound.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: It was outside the compound, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then when did they start entering the compound?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, that was later on that day. When the total amount of people was going to be a big crowd, we were ordered to let the people into the compound in small groups of 25 persons, and send them through the hole in the fence to the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How did these people arrive?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, like I said before, first in small groups. Later on they -- there was one big mass of people coming down the road from Srebrenica to Potocari. Well, they came with a big, big noise, women crying, children screaming, children also crying, well, people in terror. They came down the road towards our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: On foot?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: On foot, yes. When we could receive them, we just only could tell them to wait and to stay at our position. We couldn't tell them what to do, and they kept asking these questions, "What are we going to do? What are the plans for now?" They were very much afraid of what was going on with them, what was going to happen with them, but we couldn't tell them so -- and they were -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Had they walked the way from the city of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Most of them, yes. Most of them. There were several vehicles from the compound in Srebrenica to the compound in Potocari carrying some wounded. But when they started to move, people who were not wounded picked their places; also on every spot of the vehicle where they could hang on, they got a place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When you're talking about these vehicles, were they UN vehicles?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, they were our UN vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No other means of transportation, like buses or trucks for these fleeing people?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, some APCs for medical aid. Those APCs were also carrying some wounded people and some healthy people towards our position, and the wounded people toward the compound, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: They started coming in small groups and then they grew more and more.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you make some estimations, looking at what time they started and then how they slowly encompassed a big crowd of people?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I was ordered to make a rough counting of the people constantly. Well, it started with ten people, then hundreds of people, and then even more, thousands of people. Well, it started approximately -- they started coming around about 1500 hours, and, well, until late in the evening it stopped. So, for example, the road had a diameter of six metres and was fully crowded with people, most of them women, children, and older men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When you said you started to count them, did you do that yourself?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. Later on that day I compared with my colleagues to make a rough counting of the total number of people, and we came to a number of approximately 15.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: 15.000 people.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: 15.000 people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many of them were led into or brought into the compound?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, on top of the 15.000, there were 4.000 to 5.000 people let into the compound. So at the end of the day there were 15.000 outside the compound and 4.000 to 5.000 inside the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We're talking now about the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did they stop coming in the evening?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, they stopped. There were -- the crowds stopped. There were a few people coming down the road still, but the big mass, the big mass of people, the big crowd, stopped coming towards our position, yes. It was fully filled with these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What did 30 soldiers do to care for these people?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, during the day I ordered for some reinforcements because we couldn't stand any longer to hold the people. We had some interpreters to make it clear for them what to do. Well, what we were doing down there was the best we could, giving them some medical help, telling them that we would guide them and escort them and protect them as best we could. Well, whether it was help -- any help needed, we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: And that with 30 persons?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, I ordered some reinforcements. Later on that day, I guess it would be 50 to 60 men outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What kind of medical support could you give them?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Mainly first aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Like bandages and things like that?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: If we had some, yes, some bandages. There were several wounded men and women, also women giving birth to children at our place. We also had some assistance from MSF.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: "MSF" is?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Medecins Sans Frontiers. So the wounded, we could give them only the first aid because we didn't have more means outside, also inside the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What about giving them food and drink then?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, outside it was impossible for us to do because we had so scarce means of food rations and all that, so we couldn't give them any food outside the compound. What I learned later on is that we made a soup of food rations, mixed, mingled, with water for people inside the compound. Outside the compound, some people were carrying jerrycans and bottles of water, carrying water with them, and nearby our position there was a small well where people could get some water, so that was -- it was needed because it was tremendously hot that day, so water was a very needed factor over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The people inside could get some soup to eat or drink, but outside, could you give them anything at all apart from the water from the well?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Could you paint the picture, what it looked like when nightfall came. What did it look like in and around the compound then?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, it was like being on a scene. It was a little bit surrealistic. Being outside, these people, I slept outside, also my men slept outside. We did some patrolling that night and we had some posts to protect them. Well, the big noise stopped, all the screaming, et cetera, and all the shouting and crying stopped during the night, although little children kept crying on. The noise decreased so -- but it was very surrealistic being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Were there any attacks from the Bosnian Serb army, or any soldiers or units attacking this amount of people?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, not in person but we were fired upon with mortar fire during the day. Well, the shelling wasn't among the people. It was very close, close firing, approximately 50 metres from our position. Among the houses nearby our position, the explosions of the grenades, of the mortar grenades, came down, yes. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: But these crowds of people were not shelled or fired at directly.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Not directly, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then you said you had some 30 people and some reinforcements. What about the rest of the personnel of the Dutch Battalion? Where were they deployed during this time? What I want to know is: How many persons, how many soldiers, of the battalion in total were present in Potocari when this flood of refugees arrived?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, it should be approximately 200 men, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Two-hundred men.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Where were the rest of the battalion deployed?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: They were assigned to the OPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: And "OPs" are?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Observation posts.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. Also part of them were located in the compound of Srebrenica. But most of these men and women were supply forces so they were not fighter men, they were not infantrymen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: But the ones you're talking about in Potocari, those were fighting men, infantry soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: A few of them, yes, but most of them were supply forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Most of them were supply forces. Were any of your personnel taken hostage or assaulted during this day, the 11th?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: No, not on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Okay. Could any of you have any rest the night between the 11th and the 12th of July last year?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, for me personally, no. For most of them, I guess not, because we were busy helping people, doing some patrolling outside the compound among the people. Well, maybe you could get an hour or two of sleep but it wasn't such a rest. You couldn't rest very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Will you then turn your attention to the following day and give us an account of what happened on the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, in the morning it was relatively quiet. The people, well, they woke up and started asking questions about what was going on and what we were planning to do and what the Serbs were planning to do, so we couldn't tell. We carried on giving them medical aid. Still wounded people came down to our position asking for doctors, asking for medical help. Still women were looking for their children like the day before, because they lost their children in the big crowd of people. And also children looking for their families, those kinds of things. That carried on all morning. Also the sun appeared again so it became tremendously hot again that day. Later on that day, approximately at 1300 hours --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What time?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: We heard the noise of tanks and APCs, and I heard by radio that there was a tank and an APC coming down the road toward the compound. So the people -- well, there was panic and the people were scared, and they ran down to the south of our location. So we had to wait for what was going on then and wait for the Serbs to make a move.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: When they did, they came to our position, and also to the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You're now talking about the army, the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. They came to our position. We made a demarcation line of some red and white tape over the road and, well, they stayed behind the tape. Some of them asked for the commanding officer at my location, so that was me, and he introduced himself and so do I. I can't remember his name. I asked him what he was planning to do and he didn't tell me. Well, after that he turned his back on me and went down to his forces. At that time there were, well, approximately 20 to 30 Serbian soldiers at our position at the road. Well, their action was just walking around, looking at the people, also shouting at the people, asking questions. I had an interpreter next to me so he could translate what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Could you give us an example of what they said to the people?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, most of the times they were mocking at them, and doing that, it was a very odd situation because they sat down on the ground and started singing. They also -- they actually didn't make a move. They were just saying over there at their location, behind the red and white tape, probably -- I don't know what they were doing. So we just could stay there and wait for what they were going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Later on that day, Major Nikolic came down also to my position and he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you know him beforehand?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised him from photos in the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, he wanted to have a look among the people and he wanted to walk through to the other end of our location. At that time it was reported from my southern post, which was the last units of the Bravo Company, that also at their location some Serbian soldiers arrived. Well, we escorted Major Nikolic with our liaison officer and an observer, and he walked down through the people. After that he returned, and also the situation stayed the same for a couple of hours probably. Then one of the commanders came to my position and told me that he would bring a vehicle loaded with bread for the people and that we should make way for this vehicle. It really appeared, and then they started to give bread to the people. They also had a camera team accompanying them and the camera team, well, they were filming while they were giving bread to the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many people did get some bread? Did they have something for everybody?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: No, not at all. It was a very small truck and, well, they were throwing the bread and giving the bread to the people. My interpreter told me that while we were doing that they were shouting at the people again and mocking them and calling them names. Well, the vehicle returned one more time also loaded with bread, and also a fire truck came down to our position to give the people some water. Well, one by one, women were allowed to leave the crowd and to fill up their bottles with water. Everything was filmed by the Serbs. Then the fire truck disappeared again. Later on that day, it should be approximately at 1600 hours, more troops came down to our position, more vehicles, more jeeps, more civilian vehicles. At one time my interpreter told me that he thought he had seen General Mladic, and General Mladic came to my position. He introduced himself, and so did I, and he asked me who was the commander in charge. I asked him what he was planning to do. Well, at first he didn't tell me anything and he walked right through our line of tape and towards the people. At that time, of course, I reported to my commanding officer and I was told that I should send Mladic to the compound, to Colonel Karremans, so he could talk to him. But he wouldn't do so --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: He wouldn't?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Who wouldn't, Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So you asked him to go and talk to the commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: But he said no.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: He said, "No, I am doing what I please to do, and I am in charge here and Mate Boban tells me what to do. I am outside here and you will see what's going to happen." He told us to cooperate or else there would be -- we were, you know, told to cooperate with him, we would be best off by cooperating.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You said "or else." Did he --

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: No. We would be best off by cooperating, those were the words said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. Go on with the story, please.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Then he went to the people and he spoke to the people not to be afraid, that he should -- he would take care of them. He was talking to little children accompanied by a filming team, a camera team. I was constantly protesting that he should go to the compound. While doing that, some buses arrived and I reported that. Then I asked him again what he was going to do. He was irritated and he told me that he would evacuate the people to another place. At once some of the Serbian soldiers pulled down several of my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What did they do?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: They pulled down and pulled away several of my men who were holding the civilians, and, well, the Serbs told the civilians to go to the buses, to get inside the buses. Well, at that time the situation was taken out of our hands and we could only escort the people and provide any harm [sic] of the people. They were fully in charge at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many Bosnian Serb troops were present then, in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, I estimated approximately 40, 50 men and, well, they were still coming up, more men, men with dogs, all that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You were outnumbered.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, we were severely outnumbered. Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Okay. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Then I was told to escort the people and to provide any harming [sic] of the people, and we could not do anything else other than just escorting them. The Serbs took over and they pushed the people to go to the buses, and they kept on doing that till the buses were fully stuffed with people. They were putting far more people inside the bus than normally is usual. The buses drove away. Then we had to stop the people again and we had to wait till other transport arrived at our location.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you in any way convoy or send somebody with the buses when they went away?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: I learned later that we escorted the buses and the trucks by sending some of our men with a jeep driving in front or with the buses. Well, the first transport, they succeeded escorting them, and the other transports, well, the jeeps were taken away from us so we couldn't escort them any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: By the Serbian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: By the soldiers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb soldiers, yes. Was any separation of sexes taking place before they were loaded on buses?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, they were looking for men, older men -- well, men of fighting age, potential fighting men, and they were separating them from their families and from the rest of the people. Well, they kept on doing that the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What happened to these men who were separated from their families? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: They put them inside a house, and from what I have seen they were just sitting there and waiting. Their personal belongings were taken away and put outside of the house, and I only saw these men waiting. As far as we could, we were protesting against it, but we were, as you said before, outnumbered so we couldn't be at all places.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Of course. What about General Mladic? Was he present while these things went on?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, I lost sight of him. When the first buses started to drive away, I lost sight of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: This transportation of people started, as I remember you said, at about 1600 or --

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: That was the time when General Mladic arrived --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When he arrived.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: -- and, well, it shouldn't be more than a half hour, an hour later, when the buses arrived and drove away.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many busloads of people left Potocari this day, the 12th?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: I didn't count them all but, well, they started -- I'm sorry, they ended up when night fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: With nightfall, they stopped.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Do you have an idea of how many busloads that was? Do you have any idea how many people left on the first day?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Half, a third? No idea?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: No, I have no estimation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You can make no estimation. They stopped at nightfall, you said.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Still then, people were inside and outside the compound.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Was anybody taken out of the compound on this first day and put on the buses, or was that people from outside?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: From what I know, there were people from outside the compound because I was there. I don't know if people from inside the compound were taken outside because I couldn't see it from my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You couldn't see it.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You don't know that. Then night came, and can you tell us something about what happened during the night?

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. We were told by the Serbs that we had to clear the road and to join the people on the terrain in front of the former bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Clear the road of refugees.

utterances.speaker: LIEUTENANT KOSTER
